clinicalPearls: Serum biochemical tests labeled 'liver function tests' are useful to detect liver disease, distinguish disorder types, gauge severity, and follow treatment response, but most do not actually measure synthetic liver function; aminotransferases and alkaline phosphatase instead detect hepatocyte damage or impaired bile flow (Harrison 22e p.2633).

Tests should be used as a battery rather than singly; when more than one is abnormal, or abnormalities persist on serial testing, the probability of liver disease is high, whereas normal results make occult disease unlikely (Harrison 22e p.2633).

Total bilirubin normally runs about 1-1.5 mg/dL (95% of normals 0.2-0.9 mg/dL); if the direct fraction is under 15% of total, the bilirubin is considered essentially all indirect (unconjugated) (Harrison 22e p.2634).

Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia points to hemolysis or genetic conditions such as Gilbert's or Crigler-Najjar syndromes; in an otherwise healthy person without hemolysis it can be attributed to Gilbert's syndrome with no further workup needed (Harrison 22e p.2634).

Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia almost always implies hepatobiliary disease; because the rate-limiting step is canalicular transport rather than conjugation, the conjugated fraction can rise in any liver disease, including fulminant failure (Harrison 22e p.2634).

Aminotransferase elevations above 1000 IU/L occur almost exclusively with extensive hepatocellular injury: viral hepatitis, ischemic/hypoxic injury, or drug/toxin injury; levels up to ~300 IU/L are nonspecific (Harrison 22e p.2635).

The absolute aminotransferase level does not correlate with degree of liver cell damage and has no prognostic significance in acute hepatocellular disease; necrosis is not required for enzyme release, only increased membrane permeability (Harrison 22e p.2635).

An AST:ALT ratio over 2:1 suggests, and over 3:1 strongly suggests, alcohol-related liver disease; AST is rarely above 300 IU/L in alcoholic liver disease and ALT is often normal/low because of pyridoxal phosphate deficiency (Harrison 22e p.2635).

Alkaline phosphatase elevation greater than ~4x normal points to cholestatic disorders, infiltrative diseases (tumor, amyloidosis), or high-turnover bone disease such as Paget's; less than 3x elevation is nonspecific (Harrison 22e p.2635).

Because clotting factors (except factor VIII, made by endothelium) are made only in hepatocytes and turn over rapidly (factor VII half-life ~6 h), the prothrombin time/INR is the single best acute marker of hepatic synthetic function (Harrison 22e p.2636).

Any bilirubin in the urine is conjugated, since unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and not filtered; bilirubinuria implies liver disease or obstructive jaundice and clears before serum bilirubin during recovery (Harrison 22e p.2634).

Ultrasonography is the first test when cholestasis is suspected (to assess for dilated ducts or gallstones) and is also the first study ordered when Budd-Chiari syndrome is suspected, using Doppler to assess vessel patency and flow direction (Harrison 22e p.2636).
harrison.pathophysiology: Serum liver tests reflect distinct mechanisms rather than overall hepatic function. Aminotransferases (AST, ALT) leak from hepatocytes when cell-membrane permeability increases; ALT is comparatively liver-specific while AST is also present in cardiac and skeletal muscle, kidney, brain, pancreas, lung, leukocytes, and red cells. Cholestasis-associated enzymes (alkaline phosphatase, 5'-nucleotidase, GGT) rise with impaired bile flow; alkaline phosphatase and 5'-nucleotidase localize near the canalicular membrane, whereas GGT, found in endoplasmic reticulum and bile-duct epithelium, is more diffuse and less specific. Bilirubin, the end product of heme catabolism, circulates unconjugated and albumin-bound until hepatocellular uptake, intracellular binding, glucuronide conjugation, and canalicular secretion render it water-soluble and excretable; the rate-limiting step is canalicular transport of conjugated bilirubin. Biosynthetic capacity is reflected by albumin (hepatocyte-synthesized, half-life 18-20 days, so insensitive to acute injury) and the clotting factors (rapid turnover, making PT/INR a sensitive acute marker). Gamma globulins rise in chronic liver disease because the cirrhotic liver fails to clear gut-derived bacterial antigens, increasing antibody synthesis (Harrison 22e p.2634-2636).
additionalDifferentials: Hepatocellular pattern (predominant aminotransferase elevation): viral hepatitis, ischemic/hypoxic hepatitis, drug- or toxin-induced injury, autoimmune hepatitis, nonalcoholic/metabolic-associated fatty liver disease, alcohol-related liver disease

Cholestatic pattern (predominant alkaline phosphatase/bilirubin elevation): bile duct obstruction by stone, stricture, or tumor; primary biliary cholangitis; sclerosing cholangitis; drug-induced cholestasis
Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia: hemolysis, Gilbert's syndrome, Crigler-Najjar syndrome
Isolated conjugated hyperbilirubinemia without other test abnormalities: Dubin-Johnson and Rotor syndromes
Isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation: infiltrative liver disease, Paget's bone disease, Hodgkin's disease, hyperthyroidism, diabetes, congestive heart failure, amyloidosis
infectionMimics: AIDS cholangiopathy due to cytomegalovirus or cryptosporidial infection causing marked alkaline phosphatase elevation
Sepsis producing an intrahepatic cholestatic pattern
nonInfectiousMimics: Hypoalbuminemia from protein malnutrition, protein-losing enteropathy, or nephrotic syndrome mimicking the low albumin of chronic liver disease
Vitamin K deficiency or warfarin therapy prolonging the prothrombin time independent of hepatic synthetic failure
Bone-origin alkaline phosphatase elevation (Paget's disease, growing children, late pregnancy from placental isoenzyme) mimicking hepatic cholestasis
Postprandial intestinal alkaline phosphatase rise in blood group O and B individuals
additionalInvestigations: Battery of bilirubin (with fractionation), AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, and prothrombin time/INR; repeat over days to weeks for a diagnostic pattern
Fractionation of alkaline phosphatase, or 5'-nucleotidase or GGT, to confirm hepatic versus bone origin of an isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation
Serum globulin isotypes: IgG in autoimmune hepatitis, IgM in primary biliary cholangitis, IgA in alcoholic liver disease

Etiologic workup for chronically abnormal tests: hepatitis C antibody, hepatitis B surface antigen, iron studies/ferritin, ANA and serum protein electrophoresis, ceruloplasmin if under 40, antimitochondrial antibody, and ultrasound for fatty liver
Blood ammonia (limited value; poor correlation with encephalopathy severity, though arterial levels correlate with outcome in fulminant failure)

Liver biopsy (percutaneous with ultrasound guidance, or transjugular when ascites or prolonged INR present) for unexplained hepatocellular disease, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, indeterminate lesions, fever of unknown origin, or lymphoma staging
Noninvasive fibrosis assessment: FibroTest/FibroSure, Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) test, FIB-4 index, transient elastography (FibroScan), and magnetic resonance elastography
Ultrasonography (first-line for suspected cholestasis or Budd-Chiari), with CT, MRCP, or ERCP as directed
redFlags: Aminotransferases above 1000 IU/L indicating extensive hepatocellular injury (viral, ischemic, or toxin/drug)
Prothrombin time prolonged more than 5 seconds above control and uncorrected by parenteral vitamin K, a poor prognostic sign in acute viral and other liver disease
Albumin below 3 g/dL in apparent hepatitis raising concern for underlying chronic liver disease
Elevated total bilirubin in drug-induced liver injury signaling more severe injury
Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, which nearly always implies hepatobiliary disease and can occur even in fulminant liver failure
harrison.prognosis: Individual tests carry prognostic weight: in viral hepatitis a higher serum bilirubin reflects greater hepatocellular damage, total bilirubin correlates with poor outcome in alcoholic hepatitis and with prognosis in primary biliary cholangitis, and an elevated bilirubin signals more severe drug-induced injury. A prothrombin time prolonged more than 5 seconds above control and not corrected by parenteral vitamin K is a poor prognostic indicator in acute viral and other liver diseases, and elevated arterial ammonia correlates with outcome in fulminant hepatic failure. Bilirubin, INR, creatinine, albumin, and sodium are integrated into the MELD 3.0 score used to gauge hepatic decompensation and prioritize transplant allocation (Harrison 22e p.2634-2636).
pitfalls: Liver tests lack sensitivity and specificity; results can be normal in serious liver disease and abnormal in non-hepatic disease, and rarely indicate a specific diagnosis on their own (Harrison 22e p.2633).
Relying on the absolute aminotransferase value for prognosis is an error, since it does not correlate with the degree of damage in acute hepatocellular disease (Harrison 22e p.2635).
Except with isolated hyperbilirubinemia, fractionating bilirubin rarely identifies the cause of jaundice (Harrison 22e p.2634).
Alkaline phosphatase level does not distinguish intrahepatic from extrahepatic cholestasis (Harrison 22e p.2635).

Albumin is insensitive to acute or mild hepatic dysfunction owing to its long half-life and is not specific for liver disease; it should not be ordered to screen patients without suspected liver disease (Harrison 22e p.2636).

Liver biopsy should not be the first procedure for cholestasis; the biliary tree must first be evaluated for obstruction, and biopsy is subject to sampling error in focal disease (Harrison 22e p.2636).

Blood ammonia correlates poorly with both presence and severity of encephalopathy and with hepatic function, and can be elevated from portal shunting despite near-normal liver function (Harrison 22e p.2636).
harrison.severityClassification: Liver test patterns are categorized by pattern recognition (Harrison Table 348-1): hemolysis/Gilbert's (isolated indirect bilirubin, no bilirubinuria, otherwise normal); acute hepatocellular necrosis (aminotransferases often above 500 IU/L with ALT exceeding AST, bilirubinuria, PT prognostic); chronic hepatocellular disorders (aminotransferases usually below 300 IU/L, often low albumin and prolonged PT not corrected by vitamin K); alcoholic hepatitis/cirrhosis (AST:ALT above 2); and intra/extrahepatic cholestasis or infiltrative disease (alkaline phosphatase often above 4x normal). Disease severity in chronic liver disease/cirrhosis is graded by the Child-Pugh classification and, for transplant prioritization, the MELD 3.0 score (bilirubin, INR, creatinine, albumin, sodium) (Harrison 22e p.2636-2637).
